title: Better a mediocre originator than a perfect imitator
summary: He defends originality, citing Clyde McCoy and Bunny Berigan.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: That's a good thing. That's very true.

I'd rather just be a mediocre originator. Than to be a perfect imitator. Because I don't care how well you imitate the other person, there's somebody who's going to say, 'he's copying.' He's copying. Because when you do your thing, I don't care how sad it is, you're the only one can do it. One of these days you'll be recognized, if you don't change, because

it's original, you know. Like when I was coming up -- a lot of guys used to laugh at Clyde McCoy. He was playing "Sugar Blues" but nobody could play it like him. Nobody could play it like Clyde McCoy. And he acquired immense fortune playing "Sugar Blues."

Sure, but he played -- he was a stylist. He played it, you know, and he was the only one could play it like that. Like the only one could play like Charlie Parker. I think Bunny Berigan made the best record on "Can't Get Started With You" than anybody. Nobody could play that like him. And Billie Holiday made the best vocal on it, to me. Billie Holiday.
